questions.q:
The table shows the times, t seconds, taken by some students to solve a puzzle.

Time (t s)   0 < t ≤ 10   10 < t ≤ 15   15 < t ≤ 30
Frequency        15            21            24

Calculate the frequency density for each class.
ms: B1: frequency ÷ class width used, with at least two correct
questions.model:
Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width.
0 < t ≤ 10: 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5
10 < t ≤ 15: 21 ÷ 5 = 4.2
15 < t ≤ 30: 24 ÷ 15 = 1.6
questions.tip: Use the class width (10, 5, 15), not the upper boundary.

questions.q:
In a test the mean mark was 64 and the standard deviation was 10.
(a) Mia's standardised score was −0.8. Explain what this tells you about Mia's mark. [1]
(b) Work out Mia's actual mark. [1]
ms: (a) B1: her mark was 0.8 standard deviations below the mean (oe)
questions.model:
(a) Mia's mark was 0.8 standard deviations below the mean mark.
(b) Mark = 64 + (−0.8) × 10 = 64 − 8 = 56.
questions.tip: A negative standardised score means below the mean, not a negative mark.

questions.q:
A histogram shows the times, t minutes, that people spent in a museum. The bars have these frequency densities:

Time (t min)        0 < t ≤ 20   20 < t ≤ 30   30 < t ≤ 35   35 < t ≤ 50
Frequency density      0.6           2.4           5.2           1.2

(a) Calculate the total number of people. [2]
(b) Estimate the number of people who spent between 25 and 40 minutes in the museum. [2]
ms: M1: frequency = frequency density × class width, e.g. 0.6 × 20 = 12
questions.tip: For part of a class, multiply the frequency density by the part of the width you need.

questions.q:
On a histogram, the bar for the class 20 < x ≤ 25 is 2 cm wide and 6 cm tall. This bar represents a frequency of 36.
(a) The bar for the class 25 < x ≤ 40 is 3.5 cm tall. Calculate the frequency it represents. [3]
(b) Explain why, in a histogram with unequal class widths, frequency is represented by the area of a bar and not by its height. [1]
ms: M1: area of first bar = 12 cm² represents 36, so 1 cm² represents 3 (or FD 7.2 ↔ 6 cm, so 1 cm ↔ 1.2)
M1: width of second bar = 15 ÷ 5 × 2 = 6 cm, area = 6 × 3.5 = 21 cm² (or FD = 3.5 × 1.2 = 4.2)
(b) B1: wider classes cover more values, so using height would make wide classes look too big / bars would not be comparable; area takes class width into account (oe)
questions.model:
(a) First bar: area = 2 × 6 = 12 cm² for a frequency of 36, so 1 cm² represents 3.
A class width of 5 is 2 cm, so a class width of 15 is 6 cm. Second bar area = 6 × 3.5 = 21 cm². Frequency = 21 × 3 = 63.
(Check: FD 36 ÷ 5 = 7.2 is 6 cm, so 3.5 cm is 4.2; 4.2 × 15 = 63.)
(b) With unequal widths a wide class would look too important if heights showed frequency. Using area (frequency density × width) takes the width into account, so the picture is fair.
questions.tip: Find what 1 cm² (or 1 cm of height) represents first, then scale.

questions.q:
Jo competes in three events. Her results and the mean and standard deviation for all the competitors are shown.

Event        Jo's result   Mean     Standard deviation
100 m        11.8 s        12.2 s   0.25 s
Long jump    6.44 m        6.10 m   0.20 m
Shot put     12.9 m        13.4 m   0.8 m

Standardised score = (value − mean) ÷ standard deviation
(a) Calculate Jo's standardised score for each event. [3]
(b) In which event did Jo perform best compared with the other competitors? Explain your answer. [2]
(c) In which event did Jo perform worst? [1]
ms: (b) B1: recognises that for the 100 m a lower time is better, so −1.6 represents a good performance (equivalent to +1.6)
(b) B1: long jump is her best event because 1.7 > 1.6
(c) B1: shot put (only event below average)
questions.model:
(a) 100 m: (11.8 − 12.2) ÷ 0.25 = −1.6
Long jump: (6.44 − 6.10) ÷ 0.20 = 1.7
Shot put: (12.9 − 13.4) ÷ 0.8 = −0.625
(b) In the 100 m a smaller time is better, so −1.6 means she was 1.6 standard deviations better than the mean. In the long jump she was 1.7 standard deviations better than the mean. 1.7 > 1.6, so the long jump was her best event.
(c) The shot put: her distance was below the mean (score −0.625).
questions.tip: For times, a negative standardised score is good; reverse the sign before comparing with distances.

questions.q:
The ages, a years, of the members of a gym are shown in a histogram. Some information is given in the table.

Age (a years)   15 < a ≤ 20   20 < a ≤ 30   30 < a ≤ 40   40 < a ≤ 60   60 < a ≤ 80
Frequency                         46                          24             8

On the histogram, the bar for 15 < a ≤ 20 has frequency density 3.6 and the bar for 30 < a ≤ 40 has frequency density 3.8.
(a) Find the missing frequencies. [2]
(b) Estimate the number of members aged between 25 and 45. [2]
(c) Estimate the median age of the members. [2]
(d) Write down the modal class. [1]
ms: (c) M1: total 134, median at 67th value, in 30 < a ≤ 40: 30 + (67 − 64) ÷ 38 × 10
questions.model:
(a) 15 < a ≤ 20: 3.6 × 5 = 18. 30 < a ≤ 40: 3.8 × 10 = 38.
(b) Frequency densities: 20–30 is 46 ÷ 10 = 4.6; 40–60 is 24 ÷ 20 = 1.2.
25 to 30: 5 × 4.6 = 23; 30 to 40: 38; 40 to 45: 5 × 1.2 = 6. Total = 23 + 38 + 6 = 67 members.
(c) Total = 18 + 46 + 38 + 24 + 8 = 134, so the median is the 67th value. Cumulative frequencies: 18, 64, 102, … so it is in 30 < a ≤ 40.
Median ≈ 30 + (67 − 64) ÷ 38 × 10 = 30 + 0.79 = 30.8 years.
(d) The modal class is 20 < a ≤ 30, because it has the highest frequency density (4.6).
questions.tip: In a histogram the modal class is the tallest bar (highest frequency density), not the highest frequency.
